appraisal_events.evidence: « C’est un imbécile » (de Cottard) ; puis, de Swann : « c’est l’homme qui a épousé une fille, qui avale par jour cinquante couleuvres de femmes qui ne veulent pas recevoir la sienne, ou d’hommes qui ont couché avec elle » ; et le cadre narratif : « La malveillance avec laquelle Bergotte parlait ainsi à un étranger d’amis chez qui il était reçu depuis si longtemps ».
appraisal_events.explanation: In one continuous movement Bergotte demolishes absent people to a stranger — first Cottard as a fool unfit for intelligent patients, then Swann as a humiliated husband — and the narrator, who does not contest the content, marks the act itself as worldly malveillance, so the speech lowers its targets and reflects back on the speaker.

appraisal_events.evidence: « moi, je venais de m’installer parmi les amis du grand écrivain, d’emblée et tranquillement, comme quelqu’un qui, au lieu de faire la queue avec tout le monde pour avoir une mauvaise place, gagne les meilleures, ayant passé par un couloir fermé aux autres » ; et, contre l’hostilité paternelle, « Il a dit aux Swann qu’il m’avait trouvé extrêmement intelligent », « la seule parole qui fût au monde capable de vaincre chez mes parents ce préjugé […] Au même instant la situation changea de face ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator is installed effortlessly inside a circle that established men of letters intrigue for years to reach, and the passage closes by staging Bergotte's verdict on him as the one word that overturns his parents' condemnation, so the culminating turn confirms rather than merely softens the elevation.

status_effects.explanation: Swann is reduced to a man who married a prostitute and daily swallows the insults of women who refuse to receive his wife and of men who have slept with her; the narrator lets the portrait stand uncontested.

The same pages raise him personally as « ce Swann généreux et courtois », the king opening the royal box to his child's friends and the charming Luini magus who does not seem to notice the value of his gift.

The narrator's framing of the duplicity — tender in the Swanns' house, malicious about them outside it, sealed with « Tout ceci de vous à moi » — aligns Bergotte with the worldly médisant and against Combray's blunt honesty.

Cottard is flatly called an imbecile, denied competence for intelligent patients, and mocked for the stomach dilation already lodged in his eye and reflected in his lorgnon; du Boulbon is named against him as « tout à fait intelligent ».
Bergotte's sentence names her as the « fille » whom other women refuse to receive and whom other men have slept with, an explicit exclusion from respectable social space.
He passes through a corridor closed to others into the best seats among the great writer's friends, and his standing is then confirmed by Bergotte's reported verdict that he is extremely intelligent.

ambiguities: Bergotte's own standing is double and is deliberately not netted: the narrator's discovery of his malveillance lowers him, while the same pages presuppose him as « le grand écrivain » whose access is coveted and whose praise is decisive. The father's much harsher condemnation (« un esprit faux et malveillant », « cet homme pervers ») is explicitly disavowed by the narrator (« ils me semblaient si injustes, tellement dans l’erreur »), so it is read as characterizing the father rather than as adding to Bergotte's diminishment.

Swann is moved in opposite directions within the same window — degraded by Bergotte's portrait of his marriage, elevated by the narrator's grateful framing of his generosity — so the two effects are recorded separately rather than cancelled; the passage also breaks off at « la situation changea de face : », leaving the content of the reversal unshown, which caps confidence in E2 rather than altering its direction.
